sentences: From the hairline, down the nose to the upper lip, a single green stripe divides the woman's face in two.
Henri Matisse painted this portrait of his wife in 1905, and it is best known by its nickname, The Green Stripe.
The sitter is the artist's wife, Amélie Matisse.
The canvas is small, only about forty centimetres tall, yet its colour makes it feel far larger.
Within a few months of it, Matisse also painted her in Woman with a Hat.
Look up at her hair, piled high and painted in deep blue.
Her eyebrows and eyes are drawn in the same dark blues, firm and clear.
Instead of black, Matisse gives even the darkest parts a colour of their own.
Now follow the green stripe downward.
It starts at the hairline, rides the bridge of the nose and stops at the upper lip.
The face is divided not by grey shadow but by one green line, which makes it look flat, almost like a mask.
The cheek on the right glows pink, with orange and red along the chin and ear.
The lit side of the face has become a plane of warm colour, and the brushstrokes are left visible, so you can feel the speed of the hand.
The left side is painted yellow to stand for half-light.
Light and shadow are turned not into tones of dark and pale but into planes of colour, and olive green around the eye adds a cool note.
The background splits the same way, teal on the right and pink and orange on the left.
It carries the contrast of the face outward: cool teal sits beside the warm pink cheek, and hot orange beside the yellow one.
Below, her dress is orange and pink, and the neckline is teal.
The dark dabs along the collar set up a rhythm that anchors the bottom of the picture, and the folds are finished in a few broad sweeps of the brush.
In the summer of 1905 Matisse worked with André Derain in the fishing village of Collioure, freeing colour from its descriptive job.
This portrait was most likely painted that autumn, back in Paris.
Around this time a critic called these painters the wild beasts, and the name Fauvism was born.
Reactions were mixed.
A friend of the owners, Michael and Sarah Stein, called it a demented caricature of a portrait.
Now regarded as a masterpiece of twentieth-century portraiture, it is a highlight of the National Gallery of Denmark.
Step back and decide: does the stripe split the face, or hold it together?
